message:
Set up npm test in a github action. (#9)

https://chat.openai.com/share/c18aff35-93b2-4274-83c3-dc005b4812a2

I'm trying to set up the github action for running npm test but it
complains that there's no package-lock.json

ChatGPT
GitHub Actions is a tool that enables you to automate, customize, and
execute your software development workflows right in your GitHub
repository.

You're seeing an error message because your repository doesn't have a
package-lock.json file. The package-lock.json file is automatically
generated when npm install is run and it describes the exact tree that
was generated such that subsequent installs are able to generate
identical trees, regardless of intermediate dependency updates.

Here are a few ways to resolve this:

Add a package-lock.json file:
Run npm install in your project's root directory locally. This will
create a package-lock.json file if there isn't one already.
Commit and push the package-lock.json file to your GitHub repository.
Use npm ci instead of npm install:
If you're using npm install in your GitHub Actions workflow, you may
want to switch to npm ci. npm ci is a more reliable and faster
alternative for continuous integration environments. However, it
requires a package-lock.json or npm-shrinkwrap.json file to be present.
Here's a basic example of a GitHub Actions workflow file for running npm
test:

```yaml
name: Node.js CI

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: [14.x]

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v2
    - name: Use Node.js ${{ matrix.node-version }}
      uses: actions/setup-node@v2
      with:
        node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
    - run: npm ci
    - run: npm test
```

Remember that you still need to commit and push your package-lock.json
or npm-shrinkwrap.json file to your GitHub repository to use npm ci.

Disable the package-lock.json check:
If you don't want to use a package-lock.json file, you can disable the
check in your .npmrc file by adding the following line:

```npm
package-lock=false
```

Please note that by doing this, you lose the benefits of having a
package-lock.json file. Also, make sure to update your GitHub Actions
workflow to use npm install instead of npm ci, because npm ci requires a
package-lock.json or npm-shrinkwrap.json file to work.

User
Added package-lock.json to the repo.

```
Run npm ci
npm ERR! Cannot read property 'text-encoding' of undefined

npm ERR! A complete log of this run can be found in:
npm ERR!     /home/runner/.npm/_logs/2023-07-04T20_22_56_587Z-debug.log
Error: Process completed with exit code 1.
```

ChatGPT
This error is indicating that there is an issue in your
package-lock.json file. The error you're seeing is typically caused by a
mismatch between the versions of npm that were used to create the
package-lock.json file and the version that you are currently using. The
npm ci command requires an accurate package-lock.json to work, otherwise
it can produce errors.

Here are some steps you can take to fix this:

Update npm: If your npm is not up to date, some inconsistencies can
occur. Make sure you're using the same version locally as in your
workflow. You can update npm using the command npm install -g npm.

Regenerate package-lock.json: If updating npm didn't solve the problem,
try deleting package-lock.json and node_modules then run npm install to
generate a new package-lock.json. Make sure to push the new
package-lock.json to your repository.

```shell
rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json
npm install
git add package-lock.json
git commit -m "Updated package-lock.json"
git push
```

Specify the Node.js and npm version in the workflow: You can specify the
Node.js and npm version in your workflow to ensure the same versions are
used in your local and CI environment.

```yaml
steps:
- uses: actions/checkout@v2
- name: Use Node.js 14.x
  uses: actions/setup-node@v2
  with:
    node-version: 14.x
- name: Install npm
  run: npm install -g npm@6
- run: npm ci
- run: npm test
```

Check for npm bugs: If you're still having issues, it's possible that
there's an npm bug. You can check the [npm GitHub
page](https://github.com/npm/cli) for similar issues and possible
workarounds.

Remember, npm ci is specifically designed to be used in CI/CD
environments and it can behave differently than npm install. Its main
benefit is that it will catch and prevent inconsistencies between
project dependencies, which is accomplished by being more strict in how
it installs packages.

User
The github actions do npm 14, 16, and 18 so how am I going to force it
to be a certain version

ChatGPT
You can specify the Node.js version you want to use with the
actions/setup-node@v2 action in your GitHub Actions workflow. To test
your project against multiple Node.js versions, you can specify those
versions in a matrix in the workflow file.

Here's an example that sets up a test matrix to run your tests against
Node.js 14, 16, and 18:

```yaml
name: Node.js CI

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: [14.x, 16.x, 18.x]

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v2
    - name: Use Node.js ${{ matrix.node-version }}
      uses: actions/setup-node@v2
      with:
        node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
    - run: npm ci
    - run: npm test
```

This will run the npm ci and npm test commands in a separate job for
each Node.js version. If you want to use a specific version of npm, you
can install it in a run step:

```yaml
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v2
    - name: Use Node.js ${{ matrix.node-version }}
      uses: actions/setup-node@v2
      with:
        node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
    - run: npm install -g npm@7
    - run: npm ci
    - run: npm test
```

This will install npm version 7 before running the npm ci and npm test
commands. You could adjust the npm@7 to whatever version you want to
use, just make sure it's compatible with the Node.js versions you're
testing against.

Also, remember to push a consistent package-lock.json file to your
repository that corresponds with the npm version you want to use. This
file should be generated using the npm install command with the npm
version you are installing in the workflow.

User
They already do that but you just said the npm ci step is complaining
about the wrong version - so how can I have it support all 3

ChatGPT
The problem is likely due to the mismatch between the npm version used
to generate the package-lock.json file and the npm version in your
GitHub workflow environment.

To support multiple Node.js versions, you need to ensure that the
package-lock.json is generated using the npm version that's compatible
with all these Node.js versions.

This is what you can do:

Generate package-lock.json using the lowest compatible npm version: On
your local machine, downgrade your npm to the lowest version that is
compatible with all of your testing Node.js versions, delete
node_modules and package-lock.json, and then do npm install to
regenerate package-lock.json.
```bash
npm install -g npm@6  # adjust the version as per your compatibility needs
rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json
npm install
```

Then commit and push this package-lock.json to your repository.

Install the same npm version in the workflow: In your workflow, after
setting up Node.js, install the same npm version that you used to
generate the package-lock.json.
```yaml
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v2
    - name: Use Node.js ${{ matrix.node-version }}
      uses: actions/setup-node@v2
      with:
        node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
    - run: npm install -g npm@6  # use the same version here
    - run: npm ci
    - run: npm test
```

This should solve your problem, as npm ci will now use the same version
of npm that was used to generate the package-lock.json file, avoiding
inconsistencies. However, this solution assumes that the npm version you
choose is compatible with all your testing Node.js versions.

If you're using certain features or packages that require different npm
versions for different Node.js versions, you may need to reconsider your
testing matrix or find a different approach that accommodates your
specific needs.
